claims.sourceText: Ansel E. Talbert, 'New Air Dream, Planes Flying Outside Gravity', New York Herald Tribune, 22 November 1955, p. 1. Page image at https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: Lawrence D. Bell, founder and president of Bell Aircraft Corp. of Buffalo, is quoted directly: 'Aviation as we know it is on the threshold of amazing new concepts', and 'Our next step will be to prove that we can operate outside the earth's atmosphere and the third will be to operate outside the gravity of the earth.'

claims.nodeLabel: Ansel E. Talbert, three-part gravity series, New York Herald Tribune, 20-22 November 1955
claims.sourceText: All three articles read in full: https://archive.org/download/talbert1ny/talbert1ny_djvu.txt, https://archive.org/download/talbert2ny/talbert2ny_djvu.txt, https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: Thomas Townsend Brown is named in none of the three articles, and neither Winterhaven nor any Navy or Air Force electrogravitics contract appears in them.

claims.sourceText: Talbert, New York Herald Tribune, 20 November 1955 (caption and continuation p. 36) and 22 November 1955 (continuation p. 10). https://archive.org/download/talbert1ny/talbert1ny_djvu.txt and https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: George S. Trimble jr. is identified as 'vice-president in charge of advanced design planning of Martin Aircraft Corp.' and as 'organizing a new Research Institute for Advanced Study', and is quoted: 'I think we could do the job in about the time that it actually required to build the first atom bomb if enough trained scientific brain-power simultaneously began thinking about and working towards a solution.'

claims.sourceText: Talbert, New York Herald Tribune, 22 November 1955, p. 1 and caption. https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: The same article reports that Bell's company had in the preceding days made the first powered flights with its new Bell X-2 rocket plane, and that it was testing a jet vertical-rising-and-landing aircraft. Its photograph caption names three Air Force test pilots with Bell: Lt. Col. Frank J. Everest, Maj. Charles Yeager and Maj. Arthur Murray.

claims.sourceText: Ansel E. Talbert, 'New Air Dream, Planes Flying Outside Gravity', New York Herald Tribune, 22 November 1955, p. 1. https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: Lawrence D. Bell told Talbert: 'Aviation as we know it is on the threshold of amazing new concepts', and 'The Wright Brothers proved that man does not have to be earth-bound. Our next step will be to prove that we can operate outside the earth's atmosphere and the third will be to operate outside the gravity of the earth.'

claims.sourceText: Ansel E. Talbert, New York Herald Tribune, 20 November 1955 caption and continuation p. 36 and 22 November 1955 continuation p. 10, page images at https://archive.org/download/talbert1ny/talbert1ny_djvu.txt and https://archive.org/download/talbert3ny/talbert3ny_djvu.txt
claims.text: In November 1955 he was a vice-president of Martin, not its chief executive, and the atom-bomb comparison he made was about time and not about money. Ansel Talbert's Herald Tribune series identifies him as 'vice-president in charge of advanced design planning of Martin Aircraft Corp.' and as 'organizing a new Research Institute for Advanced Study', and quotes him: 'I think we could do the job in about the time that it actually required to build the first atom bomb if enough trained scientific brain-power simultaneously began thinking about and working towards a solution.'
